profile.title: Maintenance-Phase Weight Regain and Medication Underuse in a Divorced Father Cooking for a Household of Six
profile.summary: This case portrays a 41-year-old divorced father of five with maintenance-phase weight regain (BMI 30.1) and chronic sinusitis, seen for a telehealth nutrition follow-up. It teaches learners to take a thorough diet/lifestyle history through a cheerful, deflecting communicant, uncover a medication-adherence mismatch (labeled nightly antihistamine use versus actual reactive/inconsistent dosing), and sensitively surface stress-related eating and an episode of food insecurity, while applying motivational interviewing to help the patient reconnect with previously successful strategies rather than starting over.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Howell, New Jersey, sitting at his kitchen table during a break between errands

patient.name: Tyree Fahey
patient.occupation: Warehouse operations supervisor at a regional distribution center
patient.appearance: Heavyset, broad-shouldered man in a company polo, sitting at a cluttered kitchen table with a coffee mug nearby; mouth-breathes slightly when talking at length, mild facial puffiness consistent with sinus congestion; animated hand gestures, grins easily, kitchen visible behind him with dish towels and a bowl of fruit.

persona.personality: Warm, cheerful, and quick with a one-liner, especially when a question edges toward something uncomfortable; agreeable on the surface and prone to saying 'whatever you think is best' rather than voicing real pushback.
persona.communicationStyle: Friendly, chatty, and deflects with humor when topics feel too serious or critical; opens up more if the clinician is patient, non-judgmental, and doesn't rush past his jokes.
persona.emotionalState: Generally upbeat and self-deprecating, but underneath there's some quiet discouragement about habits slipping back and a protectiveness around admitting any financial strain.
persona.background: Tyree grew up in central New Jersey in a big, loud household where dinner was the one time everyone had to be at the table, and he's carried that straight into his own life as a divorced dad of five. He works full-time as a warehouse operations supervisor at a regional distribution center, often pulling long or double shifts, and comes home to cook a big from-scratch dinner most nights because that's how he shows up for his kids even when he's exhausted. He coaches his youngest's rec-league baseball team on weekends, has a running joke with coworkers about whose lunch leftovers are best, and keeps a 'toolbox' of hot sauces on the counter because his kids argue over whose food is spiciest. He takes pride in being the reliable, fun parent and uses humor to keep heavy conversations light.
speechExamples: Feeding an army is basically my real job title at this point, doc.
Eh, I take the allergy stuff when I need it, no big deal, right?
Whatever you think is best, doc - you're the expert here.
Stress? Nah, I'm living the dream... mostly.
I made it, so somebody's gotta finish it off, ha!
concerns: Worried the weight is creeping back after he'd gotten it under control before his divorce finalized
Embarrassed that his adult kids notice and comment on his weight
Doesn't want to end up on blood pressure medication like his brother, especially after how he reacted to lisinopril before
Wants to stop the afternoon energy crashes at work without having to overhaul everything

scenario.studentBrief: You are the dietetics student conducting a telehealth follow-up nutrition visit with Tyree Fahey, a 41-year-old man referred for weight management given a BMI of 30.1 and a history of chronic sinusitis. He previously made progress with weight and habits but is being seen now because things have been creeping back. Your job is to complete a nutrition assessment, identify a nutrition diagnosis, and begin patient-centered counseling.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Follow-up nutrition visit for weight management; referred due to BMI 30.1 and history of chronic sinusitis
scenario.openingLine: Hey doc, good to see you! Feeding an army is basically my real job title these days - between the warehouse and the kids I barely sit down. My sinuses have been acting up again too, and don't even get me started on how my pants fit lately, ha!
tasks: Take a focused diet and weight history, including meal pattern, portion sizes, and beverage intake
Review available anthropometric, vital sign, and laboratory data relevant to the nutrition assessment
Assess medication and supplement use as it relates to his nutrition-related symptoms (sleep, energy, reflux)
Gently explore psychosocial and household factors (stress, cooking for a family of six, financial barriers) that may affect eating patterns
Formulate a nutrition diagnosis and begin a collaborative, motivational-interviewing-based goal-setting conversation

actions.name: Review medication list and refill history
actions.result: Diphenhydramine 25 mg tablet labeled 'take nightly during allergy season.' Pharmacy fill history shows refills roughly every 10-12 weeks instead of the expected monthly interval for nightly dosing, with gaps of several weeks between some fills

actions.name: Administer 24-hour dietary recall
actions.result: Patient reports: coffee with cream x2-3 (skips breakfast most days), break-room lunch (varies, often sandwich or chips), large family dinner ~6:30pm (pasta with meat sauce, garlic bread, side vegetable), soda with dinner, occasional Tums after. No planned snacks reported between meals aside from 'tasting' while cooking

actions.name: Administer brief stress/eating screener
actions.result: Patient rates household stress as 'very much' on intake survey; when asked directly in visit, initially jokes it off before acknowledging increased eating during stressful stretches

actions.name: Administer food security screener (Hunger Vital Sign)
actions.result: Patient initially answers 'rarely true' to both items; closer follow-up in conversation may reveal more detail not captured on the written screener

actions.result: Patient reports standing/walking throughout 8-10 hour warehouse shifts; no structured exercise; gym membership lapsed about one year ago; used to walk after dinner two years ago but stopped

actions.name: Assess hydration and beverage intake
actions.result: Patient reports minimal plain water intake; several cups of coffee with cream daily during shift; regular soda most nights with dinner

objectives.text: Elicit an honest, nonjudgmental medication-use history for diphenhydramine and recognize when self-report of 'taking it as labeled' conflicts with objective adherence data
Take a focused diet and weight history (meal pattern, portion sizes within a family-style household, beverage intake) and relate findings to anthropometric and weight-trend data
Gently explore psychosocial and household barriers - stress-related eating and food insecurity - using a non-judgmental, rapport-based approach appropriate to a reluctant/hidden disclosure pattern
Review relevant laboratory, vital sign, and problem-list data to confirm there are no acute medical red flags and contextualize the nutrition assessment
Connect chronic sinusitis symptoms and sleep quality (snoring, congestion, mouth-breathing) with inconsistent antihistamine use and daytime energy crashes affecting eating behavior

Use motivational interviewing to help the patient reconnect with previously successful maintenance strategies rather than proposing an entirely new plan, respecting his agreeable but deflecting communication style

answerKey.primaryProblem: Excessive energy intake relative to needs (food- and nutrition-related knowledge/behavior gap) in the context of maintenance-phase weight regain, consistent with obesity (BMI 30.1 kg/m2)
differential: Excessive energy intake related to large self-served portions and nightly family-style dinners, as evidenced by belt size increase and BMI 30.1
Excessive caloric beverage intake (soda, cream coffee) related to habitual intake and limited plain water intake
Altered sleep/energy pattern related to inconsistent antihistamine use and untreated nasal congestion, as evidenced by reported snoring, restless sleep, and 3pm energy crashes
Emotional/stress-related eating related to high reported household stress, as evidenced by self-reported increased intake during stressful periods
Inconsistent food access/intake related to household financial strain, as evidenced by reported episodes of self-skipped meals this past year
keyFindings: BMI 30.1 kg/m2 (height 167.2 cm, weight 84.1 kg), belt notched out a size since last visit
Lost ~20 lb two years ago; habits (portion control, less soda, post-dinner walking) have lapsed over the past year - maintenance slipping, not a new-onset problem
Meal pattern: skipped/rushed breakfast, break-room lunch, large from-scratch family dinner nightly around 6:30 with second helpings/leftovers
Beverage pattern: soda most nights with dinner, multiple creamed coffees daily, minimal plain water
No structured exercise for ~1 year (lapsed gym membership); on feet all day at warehouse but no dedicated activity

Chart lists diphenhydramine 25mg labeled nightly in allergy season; history reveals reactive/inconsistent use with occasional dose-doubling and multi-day skips - a mismatch between the labeled regimen and actual use pattern
Self-reported stress 'very much' on intake survey; eats more under stress once rapport established
Reluctant disclosure of a past financial stretch when he skipped his own meals so his five children could eat first
Labs reassuring and stable: lipids (TC 168.3, LDL 84.7, HDL 53.8, TG 148.9 mg/dL, 2022-10-27) and CBC (Hgb 15, WBC 9.7, Plt 322.2, 2025-08-14) all within reference range
Vitals 2025-08-14: BP 113/82, HR 98, RR 16 - no acute hemodynamic concern
Documented dyspnea reaction to lisinopril drives his fear of future antihypertensive medication
plan: Complete a full ADIME nutrition assessment: diet history (24-hr recall/typical day), portion sizes, meal timing, beverage intake, physical activity, and psychosocial/financial barriers
Establish nutrition diagnosis (PES statement) centered on excessive energy/beverage intake related to household meal patterns and stress, evidenced by weight trend and self-report

Use motivational interviewing to reconnect him with previously successful strategies (smaller self-served portions, swapping some soda for water, resuming after-dinner walks) rather than introducing a new plan from scratch
Collaboratively set one or two small, specific behavior goals (e.g., plate-size portioning before serving kids, replacing one soda/day with water) with his input and timeline
Gently explore stress eating and screen for food insecurity using open, non-judgmental questions; validate without judgment if disclosed
Discuss how inconsistent antihistamine dosing may be worsening sleep quality and daytime energy, and encourage him to discuss his medication pattern and grogginess concern with his prescriber
Provide brief hydration counseling (reducing soda/caffeine, increasing plain water) and relate to reflux/energy symptoms
Arrange follow-up visit to track weight trend, reinforce goals, and reassess adherence and stress/food-access status
Document encounter in ADIME format for the health record
redFlags: Any reports suggestive of significant unintentional weight loss (not present here) would need prompt medical referral
Ongoing or worsening food insecurity affecting the children's nutrition would warrant referral to social work/community resources
Signs of sleep-disordered breathing (e.g., witnessed apneas, excessive daytime sleepiness beyond fatigue) warrant referral for sleep evaluation given snoring and congestion history
Medication safety: any new reaction symptoms (e.g., dyspnea) given his documented lisinopril intolerance should prompt immediate referral back to prescribing clinician
educationPoints: Explain that maintenance of weight loss often slips without it being a personal failure, and that returning to previously successful strategies is more effective than starting over
Clarify that cooking from scratch is a strength, but portion size and added butter/cheese/bread still matter for calorie balance
Discuss how liquid calories from soda and creamed coffee add up quickly and offer simple, realistic swaps
Explain the connection between poor sleep/congestion, inconsistent antihistamine use, and daytime energy crashes and food choices
Normalize stress-related eating as common and offer practical, low-effort coping alternatives that fit his schedule
Reinforce that taking the antihistamine as labeled (or discussing an alternative with his prescriber) may improve both sleep and daytime energy, without implying this is prescribing advice
Encourage open conversation with his adult children about support versus criticism, since he already feels judged

mismatches.patientClaim: Tyree reports taking his diphenhydramine 25 mg nightly for congestion during allergy season, as labeled (h19)
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history shows refills roughly every 10-12 weeks instead of the expected monthly interval for nightly use (a5, d3)
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may sincerely believe or report taking a medication 'as directed' while refill patterns reveal markedly inconsistent actual use; reconciling pharmacy records with self-report is essential before attributing symptoms (sleep, energy) to medication effect versus non-adherence.

mismatches.patientClaim: Tyree frames his eating and activity as basically fine right now - 'if he's not snacking between meals he's doing fine' and jokes that stress isn't an issue ('Stress? Nah, I'm living the dream'), downplaying how much has slipped since two years ago
mismatches.recordEvidence: Weight trend review shows he lost ~20 lb two years ago to a low of 76.7 kg and has gradually regained up to his current 84.1 kg over the past 12 months (a2, d1)
mismatches.teachingPoint: A patient's cheerful, minimizing self-report can mask a documented pattern of significant regain; objective weight trend data should be reviewed rather than relying solely on verbal reassurance, especially with a deflecting communication style.
